summary: This unit teaches you to prepare basic mechanical drawings by hand, to the standards the trade uses. You will learn to plan a drawing, use drawing equipment, set out a sheet and title block, draw the correct line types, work to scale, and produce orthographic, isometric and oblique drawings, sections and freehand sketches. You will also learn to dimension and tolerance a part, read basic welding symbols, and check, issue, revise and store drawings.

blocks.p: A **mechanical drawing** tells the workshop exactly what to make: the shape of a part, every size, the material, the tolerances and how it is joined. A good drawing can be read the same way by anyone trained, anywhere, so nothing is left to guesswork. This unit teaches you to prepare basic mechanical drawings by hand: working drawings of single parts, simple assemblies, pictorial drawings and sketches.

In welding and fabrication you will draw brackets, base plates, frames, gussets and simple welded assemblies. Even where an office draws with CAD (computer-aided design), the same rules apply: projection, line types, scales, dimensioning and checking. Learning them by hand is the best way to understand them.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who must produce simple drawings for the workshop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Collect the information needed (sizes, material, quantity, how it is made) and choose the views, the scale, the sheet size and the projection.
Set up a board and sheet, and use the T-square, set squares, compass, dividers, scale rule, templates and pencils correctly.
Draw a border and title block, use the correct line types and weights, and letter clearly.
Choose a standard scale, work out drawn sizes, and give real sizes in the dimensions.
Produce front, plan and end views in first-angle or third-angle projection, lined up by projection lines.
Make isometric and oblique drawings, and freehand sketches of real parts with all their sizes.
Add dimensions, symbols and tolerances by the standard rules, so the part can be made without guessing.
Show inside detail with sectional views and hatching, and use basic geometric constructions.
Check a drawing, have it approved, issue it, control revisions, and store drawings safely.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on equipment, lines, paper sizes, scales, projection, pictorial drawing, dimensioning, sections, constructions, welding symbols and drawing control.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and abbreviations such as PCD, CSK and NTS) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a three-view working drawing of a welded bracket on A3 paper, and a measured freehand sketch of a workshop part followed by an isometric drawing of it. The assessor looks at your method, your line work and your checking, not only the finished sheet.

blocks.note: Learn the abbreviations and symbols in the Dimensions section and the line types in the Lines section. Short-answer questions ask for them exactly.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Collect everything you need to know before you draw a line. A drawing started with half the facts is usually drawn twice.

ul: **What the part is and what it does**, and how it fits with other parts.
**All its sizes**, from a design sketch, a model, an old part or the customer's notes.
**The material** and its thickness or section (for example 10 mm mild steel plate, or 50 × 50 × 6 angle).
**How many** are needed, and **how they will be made**: cut, bent, drilled, welded, machined.
**Tolerances** and finish, if they matter for fit or appearance.
**The standard and projection** the workshop uses, and the sheet size.

blocks.p: Then decide which views are needed, which scale lets them fit with room for dimensions, and how to set them out on the sheet.

head: Item
What it is used for
Care and good practice
rows: Drawing board (or a drawing table with parallel motion)
A smooth, flat surface; its straight left edge guides the T-square
Keep the surface clean and unmarked; never cut on it
Drawing horizontal lines; guiding the set squares
Keep the head tight on the blade; hang it up; never use its edge to cut against
Vertical lines (resting on the T-square) and lines at 30°, 45° and 60°; used together they give 15° and 75°
Keep the edges clean and unchipped
Measuring and setting out sizes at scales such as 1:1, 1:2, 1:5 and 1:10
Measure with it; do not rule lines along its scale edge
2H for light construction lines and guidelines; H or HB for outlines and lettering; HB or 2B for freehand sketching
Keep a sharp, even point; turn the pencil slowly as you draw a long line
Sharpen the lead to a bevel and set it level with the point
Transferring distances and stepping off equal spaces
Keep the points covered when not in use
Angles that the set squares cannot give
Line the centre mark exactly on the corner of the angle
Small circles and ellipses drawn quickly and neatly
Hold firmly; keep the pencil upright
Smooth, irregular curves through plotted points
Fit at least three points at a time
Eraser, erasing shield and soft brush
Removing lines cleanly without smudging the rest
Brush rubbings off; do not wipe them with your hand
Holding the sheet square on the board
Never pin the sheet: pins damage the board and the paper

blocks.p: **H** pencils are hard: they give light, thin lines that do not smudge. **B** pencils are soft and black: they give dark lines that smudge easily. **HB** is in the middle. The higher the number, the harder (2H, 4H) or the softer (2B, 4B) the pencil.

ul: Draw horizontal lines along the top edge of the T-square, from left to right if you are right-handed.
Draw vertical lines along a set square resting on the T-square, from the bottom up.
Lean the pencil a little in the direction of the line and turn it slowly as you go, so the line stays even.
Start with **light construction lines** (2H). Line in firmly only when everything is checked; light lines that remain can then be left or cleaned off.

blocks.note: Keep compass and divider points covered or pointing down. Carry boards and T-squares upright and with care so that they do not strike people. Sit at a comfortable height with good light, keep drinks away from the board, and take short breaks to rest your eyes and back.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Sheets, title blocks, lines and lettering

blocks.p: Drawings are made on the international **A series** of paper sizes. Each size is half the area of the one above it, so an A3 sheet is two A4 sheets side by side.

head: Size
Measurements (mm)
Typical use
rows: Working drawings in the training workshop
Small parts, sketches, sheets for files

flow: Line the bottom edge of the sheet up with the T-square and tape the corners down
Draw the border, often about 10 mm in from the edges (some offices leave more on the left for filing)
Draw the title block, usually in the bottom right-hand corner
Plan where each view will go before you start drawing it

blocks.p: The **title block** holds the facts about the drawing. A typical one contains:

ul: The title of the drawing (the name of the part) and the **drawing number**
The **scale** and the **projection symbol**
The units (for example ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM) and the general tolerance
The material, and the finish if needed
The name of the person who drew it, who checked it and who approved it, with the dates
The sheet size, the revision letter and the name of the company or centre

blocks.p: Mechanical drawings follow recognised standards so that anyone trained reads them the same way. Most use the ISO standards (which British practice, BS 8888, follows) or the American ASME standards. They agree on most things; your Centre will tell you which it follows.

head: Line
How it looks
Used for
rows: Bold and unbroken; the darkest line on the drawing
Dimension lines, projection lines, leader lines and hatching
Short dashes with small, even gaps
Long dash, short dash (or dot), repeated
Centre lines, lines of symmetry and pitch circles
Thin chain, thick at the ends and at changes of direction
A chain line with heavy ends, plus arrows and letters
A light, wavy line drawn by hand
Where part of a view is broken off, and the edge of a part section
A ruled line with sharp zigzags
Long break lines (common on CAD drawings)
Thin chain with two short dashes
Neighbouring parts, and the end positions of moving parts

ul: Thick lines are about **twice as thick** as thin ones, for example 0.7 mm and 0.35 mm, or 0.5 mm and 0.25 mm.
Where a hidden line meets an outline, the dash touches the outline, so the corner is clear.
Centre lines cross on their long dashes and run a little past the outline (about 3–5 mm), but not on between views.
When lines fall on top of each other, the visible outline wins, then the hidden line, then the centre line.
Use clear **capital letters** of even height, upright or sloping slightly, all the same way.
A height of about **3.5 mm** suits notes and dimensions on A3 and A4 sheets; titles are larger, about 5–7 mm.
Rule light 2H guidelines first, so the letters keep an even height.
Leave even spaces between letters and words. Write numbers especially clearly: a 3 that looks like an 8 makes a wrong part.

blocks.p: A **scale** compares the size on the drawing with the real size. It is written as a ratio: **drawing size : real size**.

head: Scale
Meaning
Typical use
rows: Small parts that fit the sheet
Reduced: half, one fifth, one tenth of the real size
Enlarged: twice, five times, ten times the real size
Very small parts and small details

ul: **Reduction:** divide the real size by the second number. A 1 500 mm frame drawn at 1:10 is 1 500 ÷ 10 = **150 mm** on the sheet.
**Enlargement:** multiply the real size by the first number. A 36 mm pin drawn at 2:1 is 36 × 2 = **72 mm** on the sheet.
The **scale rule** does this for you: read its 1:5 scale and the marks show real millimetres.

blocks.p: Use the **largest standard scale** at which all the views fit the sheet with room around them for dimensions. Do not invent a scale such as 1:3 or 1:7.

**Example:** a frame 2 400 mm long is to go on an A3 sheet, which leaves about 400 mm of width inside the border. At 1:5 it would be 480 mm long, too big; at 1:10 it is 240 mm, which fits with space for dimensions and an end view. Choose 1:10.

blocks.note: **Dimensions always give the real size**, whatever the scale. A 600 mm plate drawn at 1:10 is a 60 mm line, but its dimension reads 600.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Never measure a size off a drawing ("scaling" it). Paper stretches and shrinks, copies are enlarged or reduced, and some views are not drawn to scale at all. If a size is missing, ask for it.
**NTS** (not to scale) on a view or detail means its proportions are not true. Use only the written dimensions.
Write the scale in the title block. If one view or detail is at a different scale, write its scale beside it.

blocks.p: **Orthographic projection** shows a solid object as a set of flat views, each one looking straight (at 90°) at one face of the object. Every view shows true sizes for the faces square to it. Usually three views are drawn: the **front view** (front elevation), the **plan** (the view from above) and an **end view** (end elevation) from the left or the right.

ul: Choose as the front view the face that shows the **most about the shape**, with the fewest hidden lines, usually with the part in its working position or the way it lies when made.

Draw only the views needed. A flat plate of even thickness may need only **one view** and a note of its thickness (for example 10 THK). A round bar or pin usually needs two views. Most simple parts need three.

blocks.p: Both methods use the same views. The difference is **where each view is placed** on the sheet.

head: Point
First-angle projection
Third-angle projection
rows: On the right of the front view
On the left of the front view
On the left of the front view
On the right of the front view
Each view is drawn on the far side of the object from where you look, as if the object threw its shadow onto a screen behind it
Each view is drawn on the same side that it is seen from, as if you looked through the glass sides of a box round the object
Britain, Europe and many other countries
The USA and Canada, and drawings from American suppliers
The side view of a cone (a trapezium) on the left and its end view (two circles) on the right
The two circles on the left and the trapezium on the right

blocks.note: Jamaican workshops receive drawings in both projections, so the **projection symbol must always be shown** in or near the title block, and you must always look for it before you read a drawing. A view read in the wrong projection is the wrong way round, and the part is made as a mirror image.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The front view and the plan share the same **lengths**; draw thin projection lines up or down between them.
The front view and the end view share the same **heights**; project them across with the T-square.

The plan and the end view share the same **depths**. Transfer them with a **45° line** (a mitre line): project from the plan to the 45° line, then turn and project into the end view. Dividers also work.
Show hidden edges as thin dashed lines in every view where they lie behind a surface, and put centre lines through every hole and round part in every view in which they appear.

flow: Fix the sheet square and draw the border and title block
Work out the space each view needs at the chosen scale, and the gaps between them, so the drawing sits in the middle of the sheet with room for dimensions
With light 2H construction lines, block in the overall rectangle of the front view
Project across and up or down to block in the plan and end view, in the right places for the projection named
Add the details (holes, slots, chamfers, radii, welds) in every view where they show, with their centre lines
Check every size and every view against the sketch, model or design
Line in: thick outlines, thin dashed hidden lines, thin chain centre lines
Add the dimensions, notes and projection symbol, fill in the title block, and clean off loose construction lines

blocks.p: **Spacing example (A3 sheet, 1:1):** the space inside a 10 mm border is about 400 mm wide. A front view 200 mm long, a 30 mm gap and an end view 60 mm deep take up 290 mm, leaving 110 mm, so start the front view about 55 mm in from the border. Do the same for the heights, remembering the title block.

blocks.note: Draw the same feature in all views before moving on to the next feature. Projecting a hole into the plan and end view straight away is quicker and avoids views that do not agree.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **pictorial drawing** shows three faces of an object in one view, so that it looks solid and is easy to understand. Pictorials are good for showing a customer what a job will look like, for assembly instructions and for sketches. They are not usually the drawing a part is made from.

head: Type
How it is drawn
Good for
Points to know
rows: Vertical edges stay vertical; the two sets of horizontal edges go back at **30°** to the horizontal; sizes along these three axes are drawn at true length
A balanced, natural look: frames, brackets, assemblies
Lines that do not run along an axis cannot be measured: plot their ends
The front face is drawn in its **true shape**; the receding edges go back at **45°**
Parts with circles or curves on one face, such as flanges and plates with holes
**Cabinet**: receding lines at **half** length, which looks more natural
Lines going back meet at one or two **vanishing points** on the horizon, like a photograph
Showing buildings and finished products realistically
Sizes cannot be measured from it, so it is not used for workshop drawings

blocks.h: Drawing in isometric: the box method

flow: From the lowest front corner, draw a vertical line and two lines at 30° to the horizontal, one each way
Mark the overall height, length and width along these three axes, at true length or to scale
Complete a light box that would just hold the object
Mark the features on the faces of the box, measuring only along lines parallel to the axes
For a sloping edge, find its two end points along axis lines and join them
Draw circles as ellipses (with a template, or by the four-centre method your instructor shows)
Line in the visible edges; hidden edges are usually left out

blocks.note: In oblique, put the face with circles, curves or the most detail at the front, where it is drawn in its true shape. Its circles then stay true circles, drawn with a compass.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **freehand sketch** is drawn without instruments. Fabricators sketch on site to record an existing part or a job to be quoted, and in the workshop to plan a job. A sketch does not need ruled lines, but it must be in **good proportion** and must carry **every size** someone else would need to make the scale drawing.

flow: Look at the part and decide which views show every feature (three orthographic views, or a pictorial with extra views)
Clean the part enough to see its edges, holes and welds
Sketch the views lightly with a soft pencil (HB or 2B) on squared or isometric grid paper, keeping the proportions right and leaving space round each view
Add centre lines through holes and round parts
Measure the part with suitable tools: rule or tape for lengths, vernier caliper for thicknesses and hole sizes, protractor for angles, working from one datum edge
Write each size on the sketch as you measure it, with dimension lines and arrows
Note the material, thicknesses, welds, the number needed, your name and the date
Check the sketch against the part once more before you leave it

blocks.note: To get proportions right, sketch a light box for the whole part first and divide it by eye (halves, thirds, quarters) before drawing the details. Sketch a circle inside a light square, touching the middle of each side.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Part
What it is
rows: A thin line that carries the edge of the feature out from the view; it starts with a small gap (about 1 mm) from the outline and runs a little past the dimension line (about 2–3 mm)
A thin line with an arrowhead at each end, touching the projection lines
A neat, filled arrowhead, about 3 mm long and about three times as long as it is wide
The size, in millimetres, written above the middle of the dimension line
A thin line from a note or size to the feature, ending in an arrowhead on an edge or a dot inside a surface

ul: Give all sizes in **millimetres**, with one note (ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM) instead of writing mm after each number.
Give the **real size**, whatever the scale.
Give **every size needed** to make the part, and give **each size once only**. Nobody should have to add up sizes or measure the drawing.
Do not give a full chain of sizes **and** the overall size as well: one is then given twice over and the two may disagree. Leave out the least important, or put it in brackets as a reference size.
Place dimensions **outside the views** where you can, on the view that shows the feature most clearly, and never to hidden lines.
Put the first dimension line about 10 mm from the outline and further lines about 8 mm apart, with **smaller sizes nearer the view** so that lines do not cross.
Write the values so they read from the bottom or from the right-hand side of the sheet.
Never use an outline or a centre line as a dimension line. A centre line may be carried on as a projection line.

head: Method
How it works
When to use it
rows: Every size is measured from the same edge, face or centre line (the datum)
Positions of holes and features that must be accurate: errors do not add up
Each size runs from the end of the one before
Only where the gap between neighbouring features matters more than their position on the part

blocks.p: **Why datum dimensioning matters:** four hole spacings chained at 75 ± 0.5 could leave the last hole up to 2 mm out from where it should be. Dimensioned from one datum, every hole is within 0.5 mm of its true position.

head: Shown on the drawing
Meaning
Example
rows: Pitch circle diameter: the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
Centres: the distance from one centre to another
Countersunk: a cone-shaped recess for a flat-headed screw
Counterbore: a flat-bottomed recess for a bolt head
Across flats: the distance between opposite flat sides of a hexagon
Metric screw thread of that diameter
Written beside a view or detail

ul: Show the number of identical holes once: **4× Ø12** (or 4 HOLES Ø12), with a leader to one hole, and dimension their centres.
Dimension a circle on the view where it shows as a circle, or across its diameter with Ø on another view.
Dimension a radius with R, and an arc's centre position if it matters.
Dimension a chamfer by its size and angle, for example 2 × 45°.

blocks.p: No part can be made to an exact size. A **tolerance** says how far a size may vary and still be accepted; the largest and smallest sizes allowed are the **limits**.

head: Written as
Limits
Total tolerance
rows: Limits written one above the other: 25.2 over 24.8

blocks.p: Sizes with no tolerance of their own follow the **general tolerance** in the title block, for example: UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED, TOLERANCE ± 0.5. Give a tight tolerance only where the part needs it: tight tolerances cost time and money to make and to check.

A **sectional view** shows the inside of a part as if it had been cut through along a **cutting plane** and the front piece taken away. It is used when holes, bores and recesses inside a part would otherwise show only as a confusing mass of hidden lines.

flow: On another view, draw the cutting plane: a thin chain line, thick at the ends, with arrows showing the direction of looking and letters such as A–A
Draw the sectional view in the place of the outside view it replaces, in projection
Show the cut faces and any visible edges beyond the cut; leave hidden lines out
Hatch the cut faces
Label the view, for example SECTION A–A

ul: Hatching is thin, evenly spaced lines, usually at **45°**, about 3–4 mm apart on an average part (closer on small parts).
All the cut areas of one part are hatched in the **same direction and spacing**, even where they are separate on the view.
Where two parts touch in a section, hatch them **in opposite directions**, or with different spacing, so the joint between them is clear.
If 45° lines would run parallel to an outline, use another angle, such as 30° or 60°.
Very thin parts in section, such as a gasket or sheet, may be filled in solid.

Shafts, bolts, nuts, studs, pins, keys, rivets and washers, and thin ribs and webs, are **not hatched** when the cutting plane runs along their length. Hatching them would suggest solid material where there is none to show.

head: Kind of section
What it shows
rows: The whole view cut through on one plane
A symmetrical part: one half shown outside, the other half in section, divided by the centre line
A small area broken out to show one inside feature, edged with a thin wavy line
The cross-section of an arm, rib or bar, turned through 90° and drawn on the view or beside it

head: Construction
How to do it
rows: Bisect a line (draw its perpendicular bisector)
Set the compass to more than half the line. Draw arcs above and below the line from each end. Join the two crossing points: this line cuts the first in half at 90°.
From the corner, draw an arc cutting both arms. From those two points draw equal arcs that cross. Join the corner to the crossing point.
Divide a line into equal parts

Draw a second line at any angle from one end. Step off the number of equal spaces you need along it with dividers. Join the last mark to the other end of the first line, then draw lines parallel to it through the other marks.
Find the centre of a circle or arc
Draw two chords (lines joining two points on the curve). Bisect each one. The bisectors cross at the centre.
Draw a circle whose diameter is the across-corners size. Step the radius round it six times with the compass, and join the marks.
Draw a circle whose diameter is the across-flats size. Draw six sides touching it (tangents), using the 30°/60° set square on the T-square.
Round a corner with a radius (a tangent arc)

Draw two light lines parallel to the two sides, each the radius away from it, inside the corner. Where they cross is the centre. Draw the arc from there; it meets each side where a line square to that side from the centre touches it.

blocks.p: The across-corners size of a hexagon is about the across-flats size ÷ 0.866. A nut 24 mm across the flats is about 24 ÷ 0.866 = **27.7 mm** across the corners.

blocks.note: Each inside angle of a regular shape = (number of sides − 2) × 180° ÷ number of sides. For an octagon: 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Welding symbols, types of drawing and drawing control

blocks.p: Fabrication drawings show welds with **welding symbols**, so that the welder knows the type, size and place of every weld. The rules below are the American (AWS) ones found on many drawings in Jamaica. ISO drawings add a dashed line beside the reference line and place the symbol a little differently: your instructor will show you how to read them.

head: Part of the symbol
What it tells you
rows: Points to the joint to be welded. The side of the joint it touches is the **arrow side**
The horizontal line the arrow joins; the weld symbol sits on it
Weld on the other side of the joint
Size, on the left of the weld symbol
For a fillet, its leg length, for example 6
Length, on the right of the weld symbol
The length of weld, for example 50; for stitch welds the length and the pitch, for example 50-150
Small circle where the arrow meets the line
Small flag at the same point
Field weld: made on site, not in the shop
Tail (a V at the far end of the line)
Extra information, such as the process or a procedure number

head: Weld
Symbol drawn on the reference line
rows: A small right-angled triangle, its upright side always on the left
One upright line and one sloping line

blocks.p: **Reading an example:** a triangle on both sides of the reference line, each with 6 on its left, means a 6 mm fillet weld on both sides of the joint the arrow points to.

head: Drawing
What it shows
rows: One part, with every view, size, tolerance, material note and finish needed to make it
The parts fitted together in their working positions, with item numbers in circles (balloons) and a parts list
A whole machine or structure, showing how the main assemblies sit together
A welded assembly, with welding symbols and often a cutting list of the pieces
A table on an assembly drawing listing each item number, its name, the quantity, the material and the size
A freehand drawing to record an idea or an existing part, with all its sizes

blocks.p: Check your own drawing first, then have **another competent person** (your instructor or supervisor) check it again: it is hard to see your own mistakes.

ul: Are the views in the right places for the projection, and do they line up and agree with each other?
Are the line types right: thick outlines, thin dashed hidden lines, thin chain centre lines?
Is every size there, once only, in mm? Do the sizes add up to the overall sizes?
Are the tolerances, symbols and notes right? Is the title block complete, with the scale and projection symbol?
Is the spelling right, and is every number easy to read?

blocks.p: When the drawing is right, the checker signs and dates the title block, and it is **approved** for use.

flow: Issue copies to the people who need them, such as the workshop, and record each issue in the **drawing register** (drawing number, title, revision, date and who holds a copy)
If the design changes, change the original drawing, never a workshop copy
Raise the **revision letter** (A to B, for example), and record the change, the date and who made and checked it in the revision table
Have the revised drawing checked and approved again
Issue the new copies and record them in the register
Take back the old copies, or stamp them SUPERSEDED, so that nobody works from them

blocks.note: A size changed by hand on a workshop copy is the start of many costly mistakes: the next copy, the next batch and the customer's records still show the old size. Any change goes back to the drawing office to be revised properly.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Keep originals **flat** in a plan chest or hanging file, or **rolled** in tubes, in a clean, dry place, filed by drawing number.
Protect workshop copies in clear plastic sleeves, and keep them away from oil, water and hot work.
Back up CAD files in more than one safe place.

blocks.note: Damp air soon makes paper curl and go mouldy, and insects attack paper left in boxes and drawers. Keep drawings away from damp walls, leaking roofs and open windows, in closed, dry storage.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can list the information I need before starting a drawing.
I can name the drawing equipment and say what each item is for, including the pencil grades.
I can set up an A3 sheet with a border and a complete title block.
I can give the sizes of A-series sheets and say how they relate to each other.
I can draw and name the main types of line and say what each one is for.
I can letter a drawing clearly in capitals of even height.
I can choose a standard scale to fit a sheet and work out drawn sizes.
I can explain first-angle and third-angle projection and recognise their symbols.
I can draw three orthographic views that line up, using projection lines and a 45° line.
I can make isometric and oblique drawings, with ellipses and non-isometric lines.
I can make a measured freehand sketch of a real part.
I can dimension a part by the standard rules, using datum dimensioning where accuracy matters.
I can use and read the common symbols and abbreviations: Ø, R, PCD, CRS, CSK, A/F, NTS.
I can work out the limits of a toleranced size.
I can draw a full section with correct hatching, and say which parts are not hatched.
I can bisect lines and angles, find the centre of a circle, and draw hexagons and tangent arcs.
I can read a basic fillet welding symbol.
I can tell detail, assembly and fabrication drawings apart and read a parts list.
I can check a drawing, and explain how drawings are approved, issued, revised and stored.

terms: The distance between opposite flat sides of a hexagon
A drawing of parts fitted together in their working positions
Oblique drawing with the receding lines at half length
A thin chain line marking the centre of a hole, round part or symmetrical shape
A light, thin line used to set out a drawing before lining in
The line on one view showing where a section is taken
The edge, face or line that sizes are measured from
A drawing of one part with everything needed to make it
The thin line with arrowheads that shows the extent of a size
Orthographic projection with the plan below the front view and the view from the left on the right
A drawing aid for smooth, irregular curves
Thin, evenly spaced lines showing cut material in a section
A thin dashed line showing an edge that cannot be seen
A pictorial drawing with horizontal edges drawn at 30°
A thin line linking a note or size to a feature
A set of flat views, each looking straight at one face of the object
A table on an assembly drawing listing each item, its quantity and material; also called a bill of materials
The diameter of the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
A pictorial drawing whose lines go back to vanishing points
A thin line carrying a feature from one view to another, or out from a view for a dimension; also called an extension line
The horizontal line of a welding symbol that the weld symbol sits on
A recorded change to an issued drawing, shown by a new revision letter
The ratio of the drawing size to the real size
A view of a part as if it had been cut through
Orthographic projection with the plan above the front view and the view from the right on the right
The box holding the drawing's title, number, scale, projection, names and dates
How much a size may vary and still be accepted

c1.title: A conveyor bracket for a sugar factory in Clarendon
c1.text: Rushane, a Level 2 trainee, must produce a three-view working drawing of a welded steel bracket for a conveyor at a sugar factory near Lionel Town, Clarendon. The bracket is a 240 mm × 80 mm × 10 mm base plate with an upright plate 240 mm × 120 mm × 10 mm welded along it with 6 mm fillet welds on both sides. Two Ø14 holes pass through the base plate. He is drawing by hand on A3 paper, at 1:1, in first-angle projection.

c2.title: A supplier's drawing at a hotel in Negril
c2.text: Kerry-Ann is on work experience in the maintenance workshop of a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland. The hotel has received a drawing of a stainless-steel shelf bracket from an overseas supplier, and the workshop must make six more. In the title block, the projection symbol shows two circles on the left and a trapezium on the right. One small detail view is marked NTS.

c3.title: A pump base plate in Christiana
c3.text: Nordia is drawing a base plate for a water pump on a farm near Christiana, Manchester. The plate is 300 mm × 200 mm, cut from 10 mm mild steel. It has four Ø12 holes at 250 mm × 150 mm centres, a Ø60 hole in the middle, and its four corners are rounded to a 15 mm radius. The workshop will cut and drill it from her drawing.

c4.title: An isometric tool holder in Kingston
c4.text: At a training centre in Kingston, Tajay must measure a welded tool holder and make an isometric drawing of it. The holder is a 150 mm × 100 mm base plate, 6 mm thick, with an upright plate 100 mm wide and 80 mm high welded on at the back. A Ø40 hole passes through the upright, and one top corner of the upright has been cut off at an angle.

c5.title: Railing drawings in Brown's Town
c5.text: A small fabrication shop in Brown's Town, St Ann, makes steel stair railings. The drawing office's original of drawing BT-114 is at revision B, but the copy pinned up in the workshop is still at revision A. Garfield, a welder, has pencilled a new hole size onto the workshop copy himself after talking to the customer.

questions.q: In first-angle projection, where should Rushane place the view of the bracket seen from its left-hand end?
o: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
Directly above the front view
Directly underneath the front view
questions.why: In first angle, each view is drawn on the far side of the object from where you look, so the view from the left goes on the right. In third angle it would go on the left.

questions.q: The Ø14 holes cannot be seen in Rushane's front view. How should they be shown there?
o: Left out, as they appear in the plan anyway
Thick continuous lines, to show they go right through
Thin dashed lines, each with a thin chain centre line
Thin wavy lines drawn freehand round the hole area
questions.why: Hidden edges are thin dashed lines, and every hole gets a centre line in each view where it appears. This lets the views be read together without guessing.

questions.q: Which welding symbol shows the bracket's 6 mm fillet welds on both sides of the upright?
o: A triangle below the reference line only, with 6 on its right
A V shape on both sides of the reference line, with 6 above it
A triangle above the line only, with a circle at the arrow's elbow
A triangle on both sides of the line, each with 6 on its left
questions.why: The fillet symbol is a triangle; on both sides of the line it means weld both sides. The size, the leg length, is written on the left of the symbol, and the length on the right.

questions.q: Rushane has drawn the plan and wants to carry its depths into the end view without measuring each one again. What is the quickest accurate way?
o: Scale each depth off the plan with the rule and mark it again
Project the depths to a 45° line, then turn them into the end view
Draw the end view freehand, then correct it once the drawing is finished
Trace the plan, turn the tracing over and copy it into place
questions.why: The plan and the end view share the same depths. Projecting them to a 45° mitre line and then across keeps every feature lined up, with no new measuring to go wrong.

questions.q: Which projection is used on the supplier's drawing?
o: Third angle, because the circles are on the left
First angle, because the circles are on the left
First angle, because overseas drawings always use it
It cannot be told without the drawing's scale
questions.why: In the third-angle symbol the end view (the two circles) is on the left and the cone's side view on the right; first angle is the other way round. Never assume the projection from where a drawing came from: read the symbol.

questions.q: On this drawing, where will Kerry-Ann find the view of the bracket from above?
o: Below the front view
To the right of the front view
Above the front view
To the left of the end view
questions.why: In third angle each view is placed on the side it is seen from, so the plan (seen from above) sits above the front view. Reading it as first angle would turn the part into a mirror image.

questions.q: The small detail view is marked NTS. How should Kerry-Ann use it?
o: Measure the view and multiply by the main scale
Measure the view directly, as details are full size
Ignore it, as NTS views are only for decoration
Use only the sizes written on it, not measurements
questions.why: NTS means not to scale: the view shows the shape, but its proportions are not true. Only the written dimensions can be trusted, and any missing size must be asked for.

questions.q: What is the clearest way for Nordia to give the size of the four corner holes?
o: Ø12 written beside each of the four holes
4× Ø12, written once with a leader to one hole
R6 written beside one hole, as it is quicker
12 DIA written on both the plan and the front view
questions.why: Identical holes are noted once with their number (4× Ø12 or 4 HOLES Ø12), so each size appears only once and cannot disagree. The diameter, not the radius, is given for a hole.

questions.q: The base plate is flat and the same thickness all over. How many views does Nordia need?
o: Three views, because every working drawing needs three
A front view and a section, with no plan view
A plan and an isometric view, but no thickness note
One view of the plate, with a note of its thickness
questions.why: Draw only the views needed. A flat plate of even thickness is fully described by its outline view and a note such as 10 THK; extra views add work and nothing else.

questions.q: Nordia's first draft gives the plate's 300 mm length and also 25, 250 and 25 along the same edge. What is wrong?
o: A size is given twice over; leave one out or mark it as reference
Nothing: giving more sizes always helps the workshop to work faster
The two 25 mm sizes should be shown as radii, not as lengths
The overall length must be written inside the view, not outside it
questions.why: 25 + 250 + 25 already make 300, so the chain and the overall size say the same thing twice, and a later change to one may not be made to the other. Leave out the least important size, or put it in brackets as a reference.

questions.q: How should Tajay begin his isometric drawing of the holder?
o: Draw the Ø40 hole first, then build the plates round it
Draw a light box from the overall length, width and height
Draw the front face at its true shape, then add depth at 45°
Sketch it freehand first and trace over it with a rule
questions.why: The box method sets out the overall sizes along the three isometric axes first; the features are then measured along lines parallel to the axes. Starting with a true front face and 45° lines is oblique, not isometric.

questions.q: The cut-off corner of the upright gives a sloping edge that does not run along any isometric axis. How does Tajay draw it?
o: Measure its true length on the part and draw it at 30°
Draw it at 45°, as all sloping lines are in isometric
Mark its two end points along axis lines, then join them
Leave it out, as isometric drawings show only square edges
questions.why: Only lines parallel to the three axes can be measured in isometric. A sloping (non-isometric) edge is found by locating its ends on axis lines and joining them; its drawn length is not its true length.

questions.q: A classmate draws the same holder in cabinet oblique. Which face should go at the front, and why?
o: The upright, so that the Ø40 hole stays a true circle
The base plate, so that the receding lines stay short
The back of the upright, so that no weld is visible
Any face, as oblique shows every face at true shape
questions.why: In oblique only the front face is drawn in its true shape, so the face with the circle goes there and can be drawn with a compass. Receding faces are distorted, and circles on them become awkward ellipses.

questions.q: What should happen about the hole size Garfield pencilled onto the workshop copy?
o: Leave it, as the welder knows best what the customer wants
Copy the new size onto every other print in the workshop now
Rub out the old size on the original and write the new one
Report it, so the original is revised, checked and reissued
questions.why: Changes are made to the original drawing, under a new revision letter, and are checked and approved before new copies are issued. Hand changes on copies leave different drawings saying different things.

questions.q: What should be done with the workshop's copy at revision A once revision B has been checked?
o: Keep it pinned up beside revision B so changes can be compared
Withdraw it or stamp it SUPERSEDED, and issue revision B
File it in the plan chest as the new master original
Send it to the customer so they can see what changed
questions.why: Out-of-date copies must not stay where someone can work from them. They are taken back or clearly marked superseded, and the issue of the new revision is recorded.

questions.q: How can the shop tell which revision of BT-114 is current and who holds copies?
o: From the drawing register
From the welder's memory
From the newest-looking copy
From the customer's order form
questions.why: The drawing register records each drawing's number, title, current revision, issue dates and who holds copies. It is how the office finds and withdraws old copies when a drawing changes.

questions.q: Which A-series paper size measures 420 mm × 594 mm?
o: A2
A3
A1
A4
questions.why: A2 is 420 × 594 mm. Each size is half the one above: A3 is 297 × 420 mm and A1 is 594 × 841 mm.

questions.q: Davian must draw the hexagon of a nut that is 24 mm across the flats. How should he construct it?
o: Draw a Ø24 circle, then step its 12 mm radius round it six times
Draw a 24 mm square, then cut each of its four corners off at 45°
Draw six sides touching a Ø24 circle, using the 30°/60° set square
Draw six 24 mm lines at 60° to each other, out from one centre point
questions.why: Across flats is the distance between opposite sides, so the circle of that diameter fits inside the hexagon and its six sides are tangents to it. Stepping the radius round a circle works only when the across-corners size is known.

questions.q: A section passes through a flange and the cover plate bolted to it. How should the hatching on the two parts differ?
o: Both parts are hatched the same way, as one solid
The cover plate is hatched at 90° to the flange's hatching
Only the larger part is hatched; the other is left plain
The parts are hatched in opposite directions
questions.why: Neighbouring parts are hatched in opposite directions, or with different spacing, so the joint between them shows clearly. All the cut areas of one part keep the same direction and spacing.

questions.q: A welded frame is 2 400 mm long and must fit on an A3 sheet with an end view beside it. Which scale should be used?
questions.why: At 1:10 the frame is 240 mm long, which fits within the roughly 400 mm inside the border with room for an end view and dimensions. At 1:5 it would be 480 mm, too long, and 1:20 is smaller than it needs to be.
